title: Lamentations 5:19–22
context: Lamentations 5:19–22 closes the community’s prayer and the book. The people confess that the LORD remains forever and his throne endures through all generations. They ask why he forgets and forsakes them for so long, and they pray, “Turn us to yourself, LORD, and we will be turned. Renew our days as of old.” The final verse is hard to translate and is read in more than one way. The WEB renders it as a statement, “But you have utterly rejected us,” while others take it as a question or as a condition (unless you have utterly rejected us). The book ends without a resolved answer, leaving the prayer open before God. Both traditions read the closing prayer as shared ground about repentance and mercy, and they let the ending stand as the text leaves it.

verses.text: You, LORD, remain forever. Your throne is from generation to generation.
verses.arminianNotes: The community confesses that the LORD remains forever and his throne endures from generation to generation. Arminian readers see faith that looks beyond present ruin to God’s unchanging reign, which is the ground of hope.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s eternal sovereignty as the foundation of the people’s prayer. Both traditions hold this as shared ground and note the contrast between Zion’s desolation in verse 18 and God’s enduring throne.

verses.text: Why do you forget us forever, and forsake us for so long a time?
verses.arminianNotes: The community asks why the LORD forgets and forsakes them for so long. Arminians see honest lament that brings hard questions to God, trusting him enough to ask.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the question as part of faithful lament (compare Psalm 13:1). Both traditions read the verse as an expression of grief, not a denial of God’s faithfulness, since the people still address him.

verses.text: Turn us to yourself, LORD, and we will be turned. Renew our days as of old.
verses.arminianNotes: The community prays, “Turn us to yourself, LORD, and we will be turned. Renew our days as of old.” Arminian readers see the people asking for God’s grace to enable their return, which they understand as grace that makes repentance possible.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prayer as recognizing that repentance is God’s gift. Both traditions hold this as shared ground about repentance and mercy, and they compare the similar prayer in Jeremiah 31:18.

verses.text: But you have utterly rejected us. You are very angry against us.
verses.arminianNotes: The community ends with “But you have utterly rejected us. You are very angry against us.” Arminians note that this verse is read in more than one way, as a statement, a question, or a condition, and they let the book’s open ending stand.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the ending is unresolved and see it as honest lament that waits on God. Both traditions read the verse in light of the prayer in verse 21, without forcing a resolution the text does not give.
